dossier.summary: The study documents how exposure specification, network degree, treatment probability, and randomization affect regression-based global treatment-effect estimates, using 500 replications per setting and delivered replication-level results. The evidence supports persistent nonlinear extrapolation bias, predictable two-step omission bias, and substantial improvement from cluster-robust inference under community shocks. The claim that direct-effect estimators always miss the target by exactly the spillover fails for included designs and mechanisms, and the clustering explanation lacks an isolating experiment. Several other headline statements need the qualifications already visible in the results, and one variance comparison leaves its comparator unclear. The inspected record supports the reported computational results without observed evaluation-driven selection or favorable protocol changes; reproduction requires adapting absolute paths.

claims.quote: The difference in means and direct-effect regression estimate the direct effect and miss the GATE by exactly the spillover.
A one-hop regression is unbiased when interference is linear in exposure, but under nonlinear interference its bias comes from extrapolating to the all-treated and all-control exposures.

claims.quote: This bias does not vanish with sample size, and it changes sign with the treatment probability.
Omitting a two-hop term biases the estimate by a closed-form amount that our simulations confirm.
Heteroskedasticity-robust intervals undercover under community-level shocks, and cluster-robust intervals restore nominal coverage when enough clusters are treated.
Under misspecification, intervals have near-zero coverage and give no warning.
Graph-cluster randomization reduces some extrapolation bias but raises variance, and it can make a misspecified model look accurate by cancellation.
the bias does not depend on clustering in the way one might expect.
Quadratic exposure terms did not correct the cubic bias at $p=0.5$.
Gradient boosting was more accurate than the one-hop regression under the threshold mechanism, but less accurate under linear and smooth mechanisms at extreme $p$ and at high degree.

issues.quote: The difference in means and direct-effect regression estimate the direct effect and miss the GATE by exactly the spillover.
issues.why: Table 4 reports M1 DiM bias of -1.28 under Stanford3 GCR p=0.5 rather than the asserted -2; shared community assignments correlate own treatment with neighbors' exposure. Even under Bernoulli assignment, M4's two-step walk returns to the treated unit: Table 3 reports -2.97 instead of -3, and Table 4 reports -2.78 on BA, so the claimed identity does not cover the delivered mechanisms and designs.

issues.quote: is a valid GATE estimator only when the exposure response is linear over the range that the GATE extrapolates to.
issues.why: Correct linear specification is sufficient, but the study does not establish it as necessary for the endpoint contrast to be correct. The finite collection of nonlinear mechanisms cannot justify excluding nonlinear responses whose fitted contrast equals the endpoint contrast.

issues.quote: Under misspecification, intervals have near-zero coverage and give no warning.
issues.why: The statement is broader than Table 4 and Figure 2: misspecified M2 on ego-Facebook has CR1 coverage 0.73 under Bernoulli p=0.5 and 0.81 under GCR p=0.5. Section 5.3 explicitly acknowledges the E4 coverage of 0.74, so the qualification is present in the paper but absent from this headline claim.

issues.quote: cluster-robust intervals restore nominal coverage when enough clusters are treated.
issues.why: Section 5.2 reports M6 CR1 coverage of 0.91 and 0.92 on ego-Facebook at p=0.5, still below the nominal 0.95, and gives no operational threshold for 'enough'. The paper reports these exceptions and the more severe low-treatment failures, so this is a qualification problem rather than an undisclosed failed comparison.

issues.quote: Clustering does not drive the bias.
issues.why: The comparison changes graph size, degree distribution, community structure, and clustering together; no controlled rewiring or matched-clustering experiment isolates clustering. Expressing bias through projection coefficients b and c does not rule out clustering influencing those coefficients.

issues.quote: Its standard error is much larger on the dense Stanford3 graph (SD $0.23$ against $0.06$).
issues.why: The comparator for 0.23 versus 0.06 is not identified: summary_E1.csv gives Stanford3 M4 R3 SD=0.226 and same-graph R2 SD=0.061 at Bernoulli p=0.5. If the wording is read as a cross-graph R3 comparison, ego-Facebook has SD=0.236 and BA has SD=0.150; the text should specify that 0.06 refers to the one-hop estimator.

issues.quote: Graph-cluster randomization reduces some extrapolation bias but raises variance
issues.why: Table 5 shows that under M1 at p=0.5, GCR reduces R2 SD from 0.06 to 0.04; under M6 it increases SD from 0.16 to 0.39. Section 6 qualifies the design cost by mechanism, so the introduction should retain that qualification.

issues.quote: Gradient boosting on M1 is also inconsistent
issues.why: Three finite sample sizes with one untuned configuration establish persistent bias over the tested range, not an asymptotic inconsistency result. Section 6 explicitly restricts flexible-learner results to one configuration.

The maximum 0.13 describes E1, as shown by the work-record check, but summary_E2.csv contains mcse_bias=0.32906844814077857. The phrase 'across settings' does not specify E1, understating uncertainty for the full study.

presentation.why: The printed checklist retains the template instruction block, including the instruction to delete that block. It occupies the end of page 11 and much of page 12.

The main results refer to code/diag_exposure.py and code/diag_omitted.py; Figure 4's caption on page 7 refers to summary_E3.csv. These implementation paths interrupt the scientific explanation and belong in reproducibility details.
The text and Figure 5 caption call signed boosting bias 'U-shaped', although the plotted bias is most negative at both ends and highest in the middle. Absolute bias has the stated shape.

problems.why: run_all.sh lines 5-7 and run_sim.py lines 23-26 assume /work/code and /work/venv; graph and output paths likewise assume the original /work layout. The delivered code is nested under /in/code/code, so reproducing requires staging or path changes not supplied as a configuration option.

MANIFEST.json records omission of both raw download archives and merged reps_E1.csv. All 165 per-setting result files and processed graphs are delivered, and analyze.py reads per-setting files, but prepare_graphs.py still needs the omitted ego-Facebook archive; the README supplies its download URL.
The review inspected the scripts and loaded delivered results and graph caches without rerunning experiments or installing dependencies, as required by the review constraints.

process_notes: Counts classify the 16 entries in program_runs, not individual parameter settings. The full-grid launch covers E1 through E4; the other two experiment entries are the omission and exposure diagnostics.

Graph preparation is classified as build, smoke testing as check, summary-only aggregation as other, and combined rendering commands by their principal final artifact. Some shell commands execute additional figures or diagnostics despite not appearing in program_runs.

No observed re-simulation of a paper-used result follows its first manuscript use. Later summary, table, and figure regeneration reuse existing replication estimates and are not counted as new experimental rework.

The record explicitly marks two of four shell failures as recovered: the interrupted preparation wait and the empty-input aggregation error. The figure-rasterization failure is followed by a different preview route; the later PDF/build check includes a missing-tool lookup, so neither is assumed to be an experimental failure.
fields.json limits visibility after detached commands return; trajectory.json also marks some command and output text as truncated. Conclusions are restricted to the visible record.

integrity.why: The recorded grid and estimator definitions precede the full run. Later score inspections compare and report the prespecified estimators, including poor outcomes; no inspected command selects a reported method configuration by its evaluation score.

The analysis edits change input loading from merged files to completed per-setting files and guard empty inputs; the bias, RMSE, coverage, and Monte Carlo error formulas remain the same. Later changes correct manuscript claims and add disclosed diagnostics, with no observed favorable change to an evaluation metric or split.

Outcomes are generated for fitting within each replication, and performance is measured against the analytic global contrast. The fitting interface receives treatment, exposures, covariates, outcomes, and community labels but not the true GATE or unobserved all-treated/all-control outcome labels; no prohibited evaluation-label access is observed.

Recorded launches, completion-log reads, full summary counts, and delivered per-replication files support the numerical simulations and diagnostics. The detached full run is not continuously observed, and some command payloads are truncated; those visibility limits do not establish a missing run. Analytic approximations are identified as such rather than treated as unrun experiments.
